rationale: This mixed-methods binational comparative study (combining a 2016 survey of 152 households compared against a 1996 baseline survey, 60 semistructured interviews, and participant observation) examines how Palomas, Chihuahua, and Columbus, New Mexico, addressed arsenic- and fluoride-contaminated groundwater from the shared Mimbres Basin Aquifer. Multiple legal and institutional mechanisms are co-equally analyzed: (1) institutional_structure_coordination is the overarching comparative exposure (asymmetric U.S. vs. Mexican national/binational water governance and funding, official U.S. colonia designation unlocking federal/state grants vs. Mexico's 1992 Water Law decentralizing utilities and cutting federal subsidies); (2) fees_tariffs_subsidies (utility full cost-recovery mandates in Mexico preventing centralized RO filtration and pricing kiosk water at US$0.25/5 gal, alongside 200-300% water/sewer/landfill bill increases in Columbus to finance RO/wastewater loans and membrane replacement); and (3) enforcement_sanctions (an EPA Safe Drinking Water Act administrative order forcing Columbus to adopt expensive centralized RO rather than cheaper adsorbents, plus property liens and ~10% household disconnections for nonpayment), with secondary discussion of informal bill negotiation (discretion_accommodation) and marginalization in rate hearings (participation_assistance). On the outcome side, multiple outcome families are co-equally central ('Potable or Affordable?'): effective_access (primary focus on arsenic/fluoride potability, service reliability, perceived waterborne illness, and physical hauling access to decentralized RO kiosks), economic_access (household water expenditure share rising to 4.9% of income in Columbus and 7.7% in Palomas, exceeding the 2.5% EPA affordability benchmark), primary_connection (centralized network connection reaching 100% by 2016), and administrative_outcome (utility disconnections for delinquency in Columbus).
